title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
gist: Anthropic launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service that emails enrolled open-source maintainers vulnerability reports generated by models including Claude Mythos, with no human review. Anthropic says human triage became the bottleneck: its models found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities in six months, but only about 6,000 were manually reviewed. Maintainers at wolfSSL, OpenSSL, PostgreSQL and curl report high report quality, while critics note that discovery does not solve patch adoption.

themes.theme: Human triage as the bottleneck for AI bug-finding

insights.claim: Anthropic launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service that sends enrolled open-source maintainers periodic security reports generated by its strongest models, including Claude Mythos, without human review. Maintainers decide whether to validate the findings and which proposed fixes to accept.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Frontier AI labs are turning model capability into security services, which puts pressure on the market for vulnerability discovery.
insights.locator: AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner

insights.claim: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team says human validation has become the constraint on AI vulnerability discovery: over six months its models found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities, but researchers manually reviewed and triaged only about 6,000.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: AI bug discovery now outpaces human triage roughly five to one, so the value is shifting to automated validation and remediation.
insights.quote: human validation has become a constraint

insights.claim: Before OSS Scanner launched, open-source maintainers who asked Anthropic for early access had already received nearly 5,000 unverified vulnerability reports with proposed patches.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: There is real demand from maintainers for raw AI findings, even unverified.

insights.claim: Each Anthropic OSS Scanner report includes a self-contained reproducer, an explanation of the suspected vulnerability, where possible the bug-introducing change found through bisection, and a candidate patch. Before reports are emailed, agents double-check bugs, propose patches and analyse root causes.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Agentic validation pipelines are replacing manual triage as the quality gate for AI security findings.
insights.locator: Each scanner report includes a self-contained reproducer

insights.claim: OSS Scanner extends Anthropic's Project Glasswing, under which Anthropic restricted Mythos Preview access to participating organisations in April.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Anthropic is gradually widening defensive access to its most capable cyber model.
insights.locator: Each scanner report includes a self-contained reproducer

insights.claim: In Anthropic's test of an early OSS Scanner version, penetration testers assessed 97 critical and high-severity findings across 48 projects: 85 met the coordinated vulnerability disclosure criteria, 11 were real but duplicates, and 1 was invalid. The result describes that selected sample, not an accuracy rate for every report.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: About 99% of high-severity findings in the sample were real, which is strong but selection-biased evidence of AI security accuracy.
insights.quote: These results describe that selected sample, rather than establishing an accuracy rate for every report the service will produce.
insights.locator: The company tested an early scanner version

insights.claim: wolfSSL's Todd Ouska said that of 74 Anthropic scanner reports the project received, all but two were valid and five became CVEs, and that the candidate patches fitted wolfSSL's existing verification and remediation process.
insights.speaker: Todd Ouska
insights.so_what: Independent maintainer data puts validity at about 97% for one widely used crypto library.
insights.quote: of the 74 reports we received, all but two were valid, and five became CVEs.

insights.claim: OpenSSL Corporation's Anton Arapov described Anthropic's raw scanner reports as as good as, and sometimes better than, human-submitted reports, especially when a working exploit made verification easy.
insights.speaker: Anton Arapov
insights.so_what: AI vulnerability reports are reaching parity with human bug-bounty submissions, which threatens the economics of human-driven security research.
insights.quote: as good and sometimes better than what we get from people

insights.claim: PostgreSQL maintainer Noah Misch said fast-track access to Anthropic's scanner helped the project fix issues before a general-availability release, and several reports came with fixes usable nearly as-is.
insights.speaker: Noah Misch
insights.so_what: AI-generated patches are good enough to merge with little rework in major infrastructure projects.
insights.quote: Several reports came with fixes we can use nearly as-is

insights.claim: Anthropic acknowledged that some maintainers have seen inflated severity ratings and misunderstandings of their projects' threat models in OSS Scanner reports.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Severity inflation can add to maintainer triage burden, so watch for backlash or noise complaints.

insights.claim: curl's Daniel Stenberg attributed an HTTP/2 upload use-after-free vulnerability, CVE-2026-92392, to Luna Tong at Anthropic using OSS Scanner. Fixed in curl 8.23.0, it could allow remote code execution under specific conditions, but Stenberg rated it high rather than critical because exploitation would be difficult and a crash was the more likely outcome.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: This is maintainer-confirmed evidence that AI scanning finds real RCE-class bugs in ubiquitous software.
insights.locator: There is also a maintainer-confirmed example

themes.theme: Comparison with Google OSS-Fuzz and CodeMender

insights.claim: Anthropic cites Google's OSS-Fuzz as inspiration for OSS Scanner, which uses language models instead of fuzzing to investigate code. Google DeepMind's CodeMender, by contrast, validates patches automatically with program analysis and testing but keeps human review before upstream submission, unlike OSS Scanner's direct delivery of unreviewed findings.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Anthropic and Google DeepMind are competing in AI-driven open-source security with different human-in-the-loop philosophies.
insights.locator: Anthropic cites Google's OSS-Fuzz as an inspiration

insights.claim: Endor Labs CEO Varun Badhwar argued that an upstream patch helps little if an enterprise is stuck several major versions behind. Enterprises need to know whether vulnerable code is reachable and whether they can adopt a fix without breaking applications.
insights.speaker: Varun Badhwar
insights.so_what: A flood of AI-found CVEs raises demand for reachability analysis and upgrade tooling from application security vendors such as Endor Labs.
insights.quote: An upstream patch doesn't help much if you're stuck three major versions behind.
insights.locator: The work that follows discovery also features

insights.claim: Dimitrios Thomas argued that AI vulnerability scanners should be evaluated on validation accuracy, maintainer workload and time from discovery to a deployed fix, not just on the number of vulnerabilities reported.
insights.speaker: Dimitrios Thomas
insights.so_what: Time to a deployed fix is the right metric for judging whether AI security tools actually reduce risk.
insights.quote: validation accuracy, maintainer workload and time from discovery to a deployed fix

insights.claim: Core maintainers enrol in Anthropic's OSS Scanner through a GitHub pull request with project configuration and a Dockerfile that prepares the build and dependencies. Scanning runs without internet access after setup, and an optional threat-model file can define untrusted inputs, excluded components, severity expectations, report formats and patch expectations.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Sandboxed, configurable scanning lowers the security risk of letting an AI lab analyse critical code.
insights.locator: Core maintainers enrol through a GitHub pull request

insights.claim: Anthropic assesses OSS Scanner eligibility case by case, prioritising established projects that matter for infrastructure and user security and that can already handle verified high-severity reports, and it manually confirms that applicants are core maintainers and that findings will reach an authorised security contact.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Access is gated to critical-infrastructure projects, which limits the risk of misuse or overwhelming small maintainers.
insights.locator: Core maintainers enrol through a GitHub pull request

insights.claim: Unvalidated OSS Scanner findings carry no automatic 90-day disclosure deadline. A report that is later validated manually can enter Anthropic's separate coordinated disclosure process, and its 90-day period starts when maintainers are notified of the validation. Projects can pause reports or withdraw, and Anthropic still offers human-reviewed disclosures to projects that lack the resources to triage raw findings.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Without disclosure deadlines on raw reports, maintainers are spared clock pressure from a high volume of AI findings.
insights.locator: Projects can pause reports or withdraw.
